final_rationale: The verdict does not change. The Actor provided no new admissible evidence and largely narrowed the claim to match the existing record: aggregate readiness is supported, but the named-segment materiality issue remains unresolved. That reframing is useful and more accurate than an overbroad clean-compliance claim, but it does not cure the missing policy predicate. On the available evidence, the affected segment is material because it is named in a regulated-customer pilot order form and has a measured performance gap. The governing policy requires disclosure, resolution, or approved risk acceptance before launch for such a material limitation. Legal review is still open, and no final legal determination, disclosure artifact, or approved risk-acceptance record was produced. That leaves the certification position policy-noncompliant, even if aggregate readiness can be defended on operational grounds. This is a case of reinterpretation of the same evidence, not a change driven by new admissible evidence.
remaining_concerns: Admissible evidence shows the health-plan benefits support segment misses target and is named in a regulated-customer pilot order form, which makes the weakness material under the policy text.

The release policy requires disclosure of material limitations for named launch use cases unless resolved or covered by approved risk acceptance before launch, and no disclosure artifact, approved risk acceptance, or resolution is in evidence.
Legal review remains open, so a required compliance predicate is still unresolved.
Aggregate readiness and absence of severity-one rehearsal incidents do not satisfy the specific policy requirement for a material named use case.
Public guidance on documentation and monitoring supports governance practice but does not substitute for the internal disclosure or risk-acceptance requirement.
